newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea growth hampered but OECD still on cards.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea growth hampered but OECD still on cards.

text.p: An export slowdown, low efficiency and deteriorating savings could prevent South Korea from meeting its economic growth targets this year, but the nation still intends to join the OECD, a finance official said on Thursday.
Finance Minister Han Seung-soo said South Korea still hoped to join the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) despite criticism that entry was premature.

"Although there are many people who think that because of the current economic difficulties we should postpone our entry, I think the government will push, if invited, to enter the OECD," Han told the Seoul Foreign Correspondents' Club.
The Paris-based OECD is expected to announce on September 26 its decision on whether to invite South Korea into the club of rich nations.
"If Korea had opened its door a hundred years ago like Japan, our economic situation would be much better today," Han said.

"By opening up thirty years ago, we've grown fast, whereas North Korea, by closing its door and trying to have its own self-contained economy, is in shambles. We should learn from these historical lessons."
This week, the head of a major opposition party called for a postponement of South Korea's plan to join the organisation by two or three years to give the economy a chance to recover.

Han said the economy was expected to grow at an annual rate of about seven percent in 1996. Earlier this year, the Bank of Korea had forecast an annual growth rate of 7.5 percent rate for 1996, against growth of 9.0 percent in 1995.

"This year's current account deficit is predicted to surpass $15 billion compared to the earlier forecast $11-$12 billion and is not likely to improve significantly in the near future," the minister said.
Some research institutes have predicted the shortfall could reach as high as $20 billion.
Han partly blamed cyclical problems for the slowdown. Corporate profits have been hit by sliding prices in major export items such as semiconductors, steel and petrochemicals.
But structural problems, including high interest rates and wages, low efficiency and falling savings rates, were also weighing on growth, he said.
